title: De & Het
blurb: Dutch has two words for "the": de and het. Every noun uses one of them.
learn_html:
What it is

English has one word for "the". Dutch has two: de and het.

Every uses one of the two. The meaning stays the same. There is no full rule: you must learn the right word with every noun.

de manthe man
de vrouwthe woman
het huisthe house
het boekthe book

The rules

Most nouns use de

About 75% of nouns are de-words. If you do not know a word, guess de.

Plurals: always de

Every is a de-word, also the plural of a het-word.

het huis → de huizenthe house → the houses

Words ending in -je: always het

All (small forms) are het-words. No exceptions.

het meisje · het huisje · het biertjethe girl · the little house · the beer

People and professions: usually de

de dokter · de leraarthe doctor · the teacher
but: het kind · het meisjethe child · the girl

Often het

Languages, metals, sports, and many words that start with ge-, be- or ver- and have no plural.

het Nederlands · het goud · het gesprekDutch · gold · the conversation
Tip

Always learn a noun together with its . Learn "de tafel", never just "tafel".

How it is different

Dutch vs English "the"

English never makes you choose. In Dutch the choice matters, because de or het also changes other words in the sentence:

een groot huis / een grote manthe adjective ending
dit / datthis and that, for het-words
deze / diethis and that, for de-words
ons huis / onze autothe word for "our"

Dutch vs German

German has three (der, die, das) and four cases. Dutch has only two groups and no cases. If you know German: der and die became de, and das became het (usually).

title: Plurals
blurb: -en or -s? And the spelling changes inside the word.
learn_html:
What it is

Dutch makes with -en or -s. English almost always uses -s. Dutch mostly uses -en.

The rules

Normal: add -en

boek → boekenbook → books
hond → hondendog → dogs

Add -s after -el, -er, -en, -em, -je

Also after many words that come from other languages.

tafel → tafels · computer → computers · meisje → meisjes

Add -'s (with apostrophe) after a, o, u, i, y

auto → auto's · foto → foto's · baby → baby's

Spelling changes with -en

Dutch spelling protects the sound. Three changes:

boom → bomen · uur → urenlong vowel: one letter goes away
kat → katten · bus → bussenshort vowel: the consonant doubles
huis → huizen · brief → brievens becomes z, f becomes v

plurals: learn these

kind → kinderen · ei → eierenchild → children · egg → eggs
stad → steden · schip → schepen · museum → museacity · ship · museum
Remember

All plurals are de-words.

How it is different

Dutch vs English

English adds -s and never changes the word: cat → cats. Dutch adds -en and often changes the spelling: kat → katten. The spelling changes protect the vowel sound.

Verbs use the same spelling system. Learn it here, and verbs become much easier.

title: Adjective Endings
blurb: One rule, one exception: when does the adjective get -e?
learn_html:
What it is

An before a usually gets -e: de grote man, een mooie stad. There is exactly one case without -e.

The rules

Normal: adjective + e

de grote tafel · het grote huis
de grote huizen · een grote man

The one exception: no -e

een (or geen, or no ) + het-word + : then the adjective gets no -e.

een groot huisa big house
een mooi boeka beautiful book
HET grote huis, but EEN groot huissame word, two forms

Spelling changes with -e

The same spelling system as plurals.

groot → grote · dik → dikke · wit → witte
boos → boze · lief → lieve

After the noun: no ending

Het huis is groot.The house is big.

How it is different

Dutch vs English

English adjectives never change: "a big house", "the big house". In Dutch you must know if the noun is a de-word or a het-word. Without the article you cannot choose the right adjective form. That is the real reason to practise de and het.

Dutch vs German

German has three full tables of adjective endings. Dutch has one small rule: add -e, except after een + het-word + singular.

title: Present Tense
blurb: Three forms: stem, stem + t, infinitive. And the jij question rule.
learn_html:
What it is

The Dutch present tense has only three forms. First find the : the without -en, with correct spelling.

WhoFormExample (werken)
ikstemik werk
jij / hij / zij / ustem + tjij werkt
wij / jullie / zijinfinitivewij werken

The rules

The stem follows the spelling rules

maken → ik maak · wonen → ik woonlong vowel: write it double
bellen → ik belshort vowel: one consonant
reizen → ik reis · schrijven → ik schrijfz becomes s, v becomes f

Stem ends in -t? Add nothing

Never write -tt.

hij praat · zij wachthe talks · she waits

Questions with jij: the -t goes away

When jij comes AFTER the verb, drop the -t. Only with jij, never with hij, zij or u.

Jij werkt. → Werk jij?You work. → Do you work?

u always gets stem + t

Also in questions.

Werkt u?Do you work? (formal)

How it is different

Dutch vs English

English only changes he/she/it: "he works". Dutch adds -t for jij AND hij, and uses the full infinitive for all plural forms. English has nothing like the jij question rule.

Normal verbs vs modal verbs

Normal verbs give hij a -t: hij werkt. do not: hij kan, hij wil. Many learners mix these up. See the Modal Verbs topic.

title: Perfect Tense
blurb: hebben or zijn + participle, and the 't kofschip rule.
learn_html:
What it is

The perfect is the normal past tense when you speak: ik heb gewerkt (I worked / I have worked).

Form: hebben or zijn in position 2, plus the at the end.

Ik heb gisteren de hele dag gewerkt.I worked all day yesterday.

The rules

Regular participle: ge + stem + t or d

Use -t when the ends in a sound from 't kofschip (t, k, f, s, ch, p). All other stems get -d.

werken → gewerkt · koken → gekookt-t after a 't kofschip sound
wonen → gewoond · bellen → gebeld-d after other sounds

: new vowel + -en

You must learn these one by one.

drinken → gedronken · eten → gegeten · schrijven → geschreven

No ge- after be-, ge-, ver-, ont-, her-

betalen → betaald · vertrekken → vertrokkento pay · to leave

hebben or zijn?

Most verbs use hebben. Use zijn for movement to a place and for a change of state.

gaan, komen, blijven, worden, beginnen, vertrekken, vallen, verhuizenthese take zijn
ik ben geweestzijn itself also takes zijn

How it is different

Dutch perfect vs English present perfect

The form looks the same ("have worked"), but the use is different. In English, "I have worked yesterday" is wrong. In Dutch, Ik heb gisteren gewerkt is exactly right. Dutch uses the perfect for finished past events in conversation.

Perfect vs simple past (ik werkte)

The simple past is mostly for written stories and descriptions. Not sure? When speaking, use the perfect.

title: Modal Verbs
blurb: kunnen, moeten, mogen, willen, zullen: special forms, and the second verb goes to the end.
learn_html:
What it is

Five helper verbs: kunnen (can), moeten (must), mogen (may), willen (want), zullen (will/shall).

The rules

ikjijhij/zijwij/jullie/zij
kunnenkankuntkankunnen
moetenmoetmoetmoetmoeten
mogenmagmagmagmogen
willenwilwiltwilwillen
zullenzalzultzalzullen

No -t for hij/zij

With kunnen, mogen, willen and zullen: hij kan, zij wil. Normal verbs get a -t here; these modal verbs do not.

The second verb goes to the END

The other verb stands at the end of the sentence, as an .

Ik kan morgen niet komen.I cannot come tomorrow.
Hij moet vandaag de rekening betalen.He must pay the bill today.

Everything else stays in the middle

Time, and stand between the two verbs.

How it is different

Modal verbs vs normal Dutch verbs

Normal verbs: hij werkt (with -t). Modal verbs: hij kan (no -t). And a modal verb sends the second verb to the end of the sentence. This is your first look at Dutch verb-final word order.

Dutch vs English modals

English keeps the verbs together: "I can come tomorrow." Dutch puts them far apart: Ik kan morgen komen. Do not keep the verbs together in Dutch.

title: Word Order
blurb: The verb is always second. Time - Manner - Place. And omdat sends the verb to the end.
learn_html:
What it is

The most important rule of Dutch: in a main sentence, the verb is always the second element (V2). Something else can stand first (, time, place), but the verb comes directly after it.

The rules

Verb second: subject and verb swap

When the sentence does not start with the subject, the subject and the verb change places ().

Ik ga morgen naar school. → Morgen ga ik naar school.
Morgen ik ga naar school.the verb must be second

Time - Manner - Place

Ik ga morgen met de trein naar Amsterdam.when → how → where

English uses the other order: place before time.

After omdat, als, terwijl, dat, hoewel: verb to the END

These words start a . The verb moves to the last position.

Ik blijf thuis omdat ik ziek ben.I stay home because I am sick.
omdat ik ben ziek

Other verb forms also go to the end

and collect at the end of the main sentence.

Ik heb gisteren een boek gekocht.I bought a book yesterday.

How it is different

Dutch vs English

English always keeps subject + verb + object: "Tomorrow I go...". Dutch must swap: Morgen ga ik.... Forgetting this swap is the clearest sign of non-native Dutch. Practise it until it is automatic.

Main clause vs subordinate clause

Two systems in one language. : verb second. Subordinate clause: verb last. The connecting word decides: want keeps the verb second, omdat sends it to the end. Both mean "because".

title: Niet vs Geen
blurb: English has one "not". Dutch has two: niet and geen.
learn_html:
What it is

Dutch has two words for "not". geen a with een or with no . niet negates everything else.

The rules

geen replaces een (or a missing article)

Ik heb een auto. → Ik heb geen auto.I have a car. → I have no car.
Wij drinken koffie. → Wij drinken geen koffie.We drink coffee. → We do not drink coffee.

niet for verbs, adjectives and things

Ik werk niet.I do not work.
De film is niet leuk.The film is not fun.
Dat is niet mijn tas.That is not my bag.
Ik ga niet naar het feest.I am not going to the party.
Quick test

Can you say "a" or "any" before the noun in English? Then use geen. "I don't have a car" → geen auto.

Where does niet stand?

Usually near the end, but before adjectives, , and verb forms at the end.

Ik heb het boek niet gelezen.I have not read the book.

How it is different

Dutch vs English "not / no"

English "no" + noun ("I have no money") works like geen. English "not" works like niet. But English usually says "don't have a...", so you do not see the difference. Dutch makes you choose in every sentence.

The trap: definite nouns

geen can never stand before de, het, mijn or deze. "Not my bag" = niet mijn tas, never geen mijn tas.

title: Pronouns & Possessives
blurb: mij or ik? ons or onze? The forms you must keep apart.
learn_html:
What it is

Dutch come in three sets: (ik, jij, hij...), (mij, jou, hem...) and (mijn, jouw, zijn...).

The rules

SubjectObjectPossessive
ikmij (me)mijn
jijjou (je)jouw (je)
hijhemzijn
zij (she)haarhaar
uuuw
wijonsons / onze
julliejulliejullie
zij (they)hen / hun / zehun

ons or onze?

The only possessive that changes with the noun. Het-words take ons, de-words take onze. All plurals take onze.

ons huishet-word: ons
onze autode-word: onze

jou or jouw?

One letter, a different job. jou = you (object). jouw = your (possessive).

Full form and short form

jij/je · zij/ze · wij/we · mijn/m'n. Use the full form for emphasis or contrast.

How it is different

Dutch vs English

English "you / your" works for one person, for many people, and in formal speech. Dutch splits it three ways: jij/jou/jouw, jullie, and formal u/uw.

English "our" never changes. Dutch ons/onze depends on de or het. One more reason to learn the articles well.

title: Comparatives & Superlatives
blurb: -er and -st for all adjectives, also long ones. And dan vs als.
learn_html:
What it is

Comparing things: groot → groter → grootst (big → bigger → biggest). Dutch uses endings for almost all , long or short.

The rules

: + er

Dutch does not use "more" the way English does.

kleiner · mooier · interessantersmaller · more beautiful · more interesting

Ends in -r? Add -der

duur → duurder · lekker → lekkerder · ver → verder

: + st

Before a noun it also gets the adjective -e.

kleinst · mooist
de kleinste stad · het mooiste huisthe smallest city · the most beautiful house

: learn these

goed - beter - bestgood - better - best
veel - meer - meestmuch - more - most
weinig - minder - minstlittle - less - least
graag - liever - liefstgladly - rather - most of all

dan or als?

groter danbigger than (different)
net zo groot alsas big as (equal)

How it is different

Dutch vs English

English switches to "more / most" for long adjectives: "more interesting". Dutch keeps the ending: interessanter. Saying meer interessant is a classic mistake of English speakers.

Comparatives vs normal adjectives

Before a noun, comparatives and superlatives still follow the normal -e rule: een grotere stad, de grootste stad. Two systems, one on top of the other.

title: Separable Verbs
blurb: opstaan, meenemen, uitnodigen: verbs that break in two parts.
learn_html:
What it is

Many Dutch verbs are a + a verb: op + staan = opstaan (to get up). In a main sentence the verb splits: the verb part is in position 2, and the particle goes to the end.

Ik sta elke dag om zeven uur op.I get up at seven every day.

The rules

Main sentence: split

Verb in position 2, particle at the end.

Zij nodigt de buren uit.She invites the neighbours.

: one word again

The whole verb goes to the end, in one piece.

...omdat ik om zeven uur opsta....because I get up at seven.

: ge- goes in the middle

Particle + ge + participle.

opgestaan · uitgenodigd · meegenomen
geopstaan

With a : one word at the end

Ik moet vroeg opstaan.I must get up early.
How to spot one

The is on the particle: ÓPstaan. like be-, ver- and ont- have no stress and never split.

How it is different

Dutch vs English

English "pick up" can also split: "pick it up". But English never puts the parts back into one word, and never puts anything inside the verb. Dutch does both: opsta (subordinate clause), opgestaan (ge- inside).

Separable vs inseparable verbs

betalen, vertrekken, ontmoeten look similar but never split, and their participle has no ge-: betaald, not gebetaald. The stress tells you which is which.

title: Imperfectum (Past Simple)
blurb: The past tense for stories: werkte, ging, was.
learn_html:
What it is

The imperfectum (ik werkte, ik ging) is the simple past. In conversation, Dutch often prefers the perfect (ik heb gewerkt). Use the imperfectum for stories, descriptions and repeated situations in the past.

Vroeger woonde ik in Utrecht en werkte ik in een winkel.I used to live in Utrecht and worked in a shop.

The rules

: stem + te(n) or de(n)

The same 't kofschip rule as the . Stem ends in t, k, f, s, ch or p: add -te. All other stems: add -de.

werken → werkte, werkten-te after a 't kofschip sound
wonen → woonde, woonden-de after other sounds

Only two forms

: ik/jij/hij werkte. : wij/jullie/zij werkten. No extra -t for jij or hij.

: new vowel, learn them

gaan → ging · komen → kwam · eten → at
drinken → dronk · kopen → kocht

The two most important

You use these all the time.

zijn → was, warento be → was, were
hebben → had, haddento have → had

Spelling notes

praten → praattewrite tt, you hear one t
reizen → reisdethe underlying z chooses -de, not -te

How it is different

Imperfectum vs perfect

One finished event in conversation: use the perfect. Ik heb gisteren gewerkt. Background, description and repetition: use the imperfectum. Het regende en ik was moe. (It rained and I was tired.) Not sure? Speaking: perfect. Telling a story: imperfectum.

Dutch vs English

English uses the simple past everywhere: "I worked yesterday." Do not copy that habit. Ik werkte gisteren sounds like the start of a story, not a normal sentence about yesterday.

title: Er
blurb: The hardest small word in Dutch: er zit, ik heb er twee, ik denk eraan.
learn_html:
What it is

Er is a small word without . It has several different jobs. English sometimes uses "there" for it, but often has no word for it at all. That is why er is difficult.

The rules

Er +

A sentence about "a ..." or "some ..." starts with er.

Er zit een kat in de tuin.There is a cat in the garden.
Er zijn veel mensen.There are many people.
Een kat zit in de tuin.er is needed here

Er + number

With a number, er replaces the . Do not repeat the noun.

Ik heb er twee."How many children do you have?" I have two.
Ik heb twee.incomplete
Ik heb er twee kinderen.do not repeat the noun

Er + : one word

"Preposition + it" becomes one word.

Ik denk eraan.I think about it.
Ik wacht erop.I wait for it.
met → ermee · tot → ertoesome prepositions change

Er = there (place, no stress)

Ik woon er al tien jaar.I have lived there for ten years.

Stressed "there" is daar.

How it is different

Er vs English "there"

English "there is / there are" matches the first use of er. But English has nothing like ik heb er twee or eraan / erop. Learn those as Dutch habits. Do not try to translate them.

er vs daar

daar has stress and points at a place: "THERE, not here". er has no stress and is neutral. Could you point your finger while saying it? Then use daar.

title: Conjunctions & Relative Clauses
blurb: want vs omdat, toen vs als, and the words die, dat, wat.
learn_html:
What it is

Two related systems: small words that connect sentences (want, omdat, toen, als), and the words that start a (die, dat, wat). Grammar decides the choice, not meaning.

The rules

die or dat? The decides

De-words take die, het-words take dat. All plurals take die.

de man die daar looptthe man who walks there
het boek dat ik leesthe book that I read

wat after alles, iets, niets, het enige

Also when there is no noun at all.

Alles wat hij zegt, is waar.Everything he says is true.
Dat is precies wat ik bedoel.That is exactly what I mean.

want or omdat? Both mean "because"

want: normal word order follows. omdat: the verb goes to the end.

Ik blijf thuis, want ik ben ziek.verb in the normal place
Ik blijf thuis omdat ik ziek ben.verb at the end

toen or als?

toen: one event or period in the past. als: present, future and repeated situations. "When" about the past is almost always toen.

Toen ik klein was...when I was small (past)
Als het regent, blijf ik thuis.when it rains (repeated)

How it is different

die/dat vs English "who / which / that"

English chooses by person or thing (who / which). Dutch chooses by article (die / dat). A person can be dat (het meisje dat...) and a thing can be die (de tafel die...). It is pure grammar: one more reason to learn every noun with its article.

want/omdat and word order

want and omdat mean the same, but they need different word orders. Listen to where the verb goes: then you know which word fits. See the Word Order topic.

title: Om ... te + Infinitive
blurb: om brood te kopen, ik probeer te komen: how to link a second verb.
learn_html:
What it is

Dutch links a second verb with te + . For a goal ("in order to"), Dutch uses om ... te + infinitive.

Ik ga naar de winkel om brood te kopen.I go to the shop to buy bread.

The rules

Goal: om + rest + te + infinitive

Everything stands at the end of the .

Zij spaart geld om een auto te kopen.She saves money to buy a car.
om kopen een auto

Many verbs link with te

For example: proberen, vergeten, hopen, beginnen, beloven, hoeven.

Ik probeer te komen.I try to come.
Je hoeft niet te betalen.You do not have to pay.

: te goes inside

om vroeg op te staanto get up early
Ik probeer een paraplu mee te nemen.I try to bring an umbrella.
te opstaan

: no te

Ik kan komen.I can come.
Ik kan te komen.

How it is different

Dutch te vs English "to"

English puts "to" before almost every linked verb. Dutch has three levels: modal verbs take nothing (ik wil gaan), many verbs take te (ik probeer te gaan), and a goal takes the full om ... te frame. Mixing these levels is the classic mistake.

vs Separable Verbs

Main sentence: the goes to the end (ik sta op). te-construction: te lands inside the verb (om op te staan). The same verb, a third behaviour.

title: Diminutives
blurb: -je, -tje, -pje: the small endings the Dutch use all the time.
learn_html:
What it is

Dutch puts -je endings on . The meaning: small, but also nice, cosy or informal. Daily Dutch is full of them. The ending follows the sound of the word.

een biertjea beer
een uurtjeabout an hour
een broodjea bread roll

The rules

-je after most

huis → huisje · boek → boekje

-tje after a , or after l, n, r with a long vowel

auto → autootje · stoel → stoeltje · deur → deurtje

-etje after l, m, n, r, ng with a short vowel

The consonant doubles.

man → mannetje · ster → sterretje · brug → bruggetje

-pje after m

Except the short-vowel cases above.

boom → boompje · film → filmpje

-kje for -ing

koning → koninkje · ketting → kettinkje

Spelling protects the vowel

glas → glaasje · schip → scheepje
Remember

Every diminutive is a het-word: het huisje, het meisje, het biertje. No exceptions.

How it is different

Dutch vs English

English almost never does this ("doggie", "birdie"). Dutch uses diminutives all the time, in a neutral way. Een kaartje is simply a ticket. Een momentje is simply a moment. Learning them opens up a big part of everyday speech.

vs De & Het

The diminutive is the one place where is free: whatever the base noun was, the diminutive is het. De vrouw, but het vrouwtje.

title: Prepositions of Place & Time
blurb: op maandag, om negen uur, aan de muur: the small words of place and time.
learn_html:
What it is

Dutch rarely match English one to one. English "at" alone can be om (time), op (school), aan (the seaside) or bij (a person's house). Learn them in combinations, not as single words.

The rules

Place

op de tafelon the table (flat surface)
aan de muuron the wall (vertical contact)
in de kastin the cupboard (inside)

Also: onder (under), boven (above), naast (next to), tussen (between), achter (behind), voor (in front of), bij (at, near).

Time: a fixed pattern

om negen uurom + clock time
op maandag · op 12 juliop + day or date
in januari · in de winter · in 2010in + month, season, year

More time words

over tien minutenten minutes from now
naafter an event
sinds · tijdenssince · during

Fixed combinations: learn them as one piece

op school · op de markt · aan zeeat school · at the market · at the seaside
naar huis · thuis(going) home · at home

How it is different

Dutch vs English

English "in ten minutes" is Dutch over tien minuten. English "at school" is op school. Always translate the whole combination, never the single word.

vs the Er topic

When the of a preposition becomes "it", the preposition joins with er: op becomes erop, met becomes ermee. The combinations you learn here come back in that system.

title: Passive Voice
blurb: wordt gebouwd, is gebouwd, werd gebouwd: when the subject receives the action.
learn_html:
What it is

In a sentence the receives the action. Dutch builds it with worden + . The doer gets door.

Het huis wordt gebouwd.The house is being built.

The rules

Present: worden + participle

worden normally: ik word, hij wordt, wij worden.

De brief wordt geschreven.The letter is being written.
De huizen worden gebouwd.The houses are being built.

Past (stories): werd / werden + participle

Het museum werd in 1885 gebouwd.The museum was built in 1885.

Perfect passive: zijn, never hebben

No extra "geworden" is needed.

Het huis is gebouwd.The house has been built.
Het huis heeft gebouwd.

The doer: door

Het boek is door de leraar geschreven.The book was written by the teacher.
van de leraar

How it is different

Dutch vs English

English uses "to be" for every passive: "is built", "was built". Dutch uses two verbs: worden when the action is still happening, zijn when it is finished. Het huis wordt gebouwd = is being built. Het huis is gebouwd = has been built. Mixing them changes the meaning.

vs the Perfect Tense topic

is gebouwd looks like a normal perfect with zijn. But here zijn does not mean movement or change: it is simply how the passive is completed. The pattern to recognise: subject + zijn + participle = often a finished passive.
